# Provenance, Consensus and the Edge: A Unified Architecture for Human-Centred Community Intelligence

**Author:** Michael James Despott
**Status:** Open discussion draft, generated by the pipeline from five draft concepts. Not peer reviewed.
**Date:** 2026-11-27

> **Read this first.** This is a design paper, not a clinical, financial or legal document. All scenarios are illustrative and educational. Nothing here is medical advice, investment advice, or a claim that any described system is safe, effective or validated. Figures quoted from the source drafts are design targets, not measured results.

## Abstract

Five draft concepts in this repository look, at first glance, like five unrelated projects: a recycling foundry run by people who have been homeless, a local-first AI companion architecture, a multi-agent consensus model for mental health services, a phone-mesh compute network, and an automated trading system. Read together, they share a single architecture. Each one tries to (1) keep the sacred or sensitive part of a system local and small, (2) reach outward only for what it lacks, (3) settle disagreement through structured consensus rather than a single authority, and (4) make value and provenance visible so trust can be earned rather than assumed. This paper names that shared pattern, maps each draft onto it, and sets out the open questions and failure modes that would have to be answered before any of it touched real people, real patients or real money.

## 1. The five source concepts

**1.1 Community Foundry** (*draft-concepts/Proof of Concept: Community Foundry*). A rural collective where people with lived experience of homelessness collect cans and bottles, melt aluminium into ingots and castings, reuse glass as preserve jars, and sell limited editions whose value comes from their story. Its security model is voice-first, uses a passphrase with shard recovery instead of a phone number, and stores no identity. Its governance is open source, refereed by an AI consensus engine, and takes democratic input from participants, advocates, support workers and the public.

**1.2 AI Design Architecture** (*draft-concepts/AI DESIGN ARCHITECTURE AND CHAT ARA 5*). A four-part layout for a personal AI: a protected local core that holds history and tone and is never overwritten; a local mirror on a second device for redundancy; a remote "knowledge layer" consulted only when the local core decides it needs something; and a thin bridging and consensus logic that decides when to reach out. The draft also compares synthetic reasoning-data pipelines (stratified seed sampling, filtering by reasoning depth). Only the architectural content of that draft is used here.

**1.3 Hospital Agentic Consensus Model** (*draft-concepts/Full hospital agentic concensus model*). A proposed "human-centred clinical intelligence system" for mental health services. It has a structured associative knowledge layer (linked relational records instead of giant weights), a panel of discipline-specific agents (psychiatry, psychology, nursing, social work, occupational therapy) that deliberate and vote, multi-source inputs (de-identified records, notes, patient journaling apps, wearables), an at-a-glance gauge dashboard, voice documentation, and a patient companion. Its stated spine is "technology must serve people without diminishing them".

**1.4 Mobile AI Compute** (*draft-concepts/MOBILE AI COMPUTE*). A simple Python, local-first node for phones: a small quantised model, SQLite with a vector extension for "Access-database-style" content linking, a throttled background worker (around 5% idle, 10 to 20% active), gossip-based mesh routing to peers that hold relevant content, and a contribution ledger that rewards donated compute and storage.

**1.5 System Description V3** (*draft-concepts/SYSTEM DESCRIPTION v3*). A draft explaining an automated trading approach built on random-walk ideas: many overlapping buy and sell orders whose averages net out, a bet on consolidation phases, and hedging to keep drawdown small. The draft itself discusses martingale-style doubling and why it is dangerous.

## 2. The shared pattern

Strip the domains away and the same four moves recur.

**Move 1: a small, protected core.** The companion's "local core", the phone node's SQLite store, the foundry's no-identity sessions and the hospital model's structured knowledge layer are all the same idea. Keep the part that matters, whether that is memory, identity or clinical context, small, local, inspectable and hard to overwrite. Linked records measured in megabytes are easier to audit than billions of opaque weights.

**Move 2: reach outward only on demand.** The companion pulls from the remote knowledge layer and then "drops back". The phone node gossips a query to peers only when local knowledge runs out. The foundry draws raw material from the street and returns finished goods to it. In each case the boundary is a decision point, and the default is not to cross it.

**Move 3: consensus instead of a single oracle.** The hospital panel of agents challenges itself and votes. The foundry's consensus engine referees contributions. The companion's bridging logic weighs local against remote knowledge. Even the trading draft is about many small, overlapping positions averaging out rather than one big call. The common belief is that structured disagreement among several perspectives beats one confident voice.

**Move 4: visible provenance and fair value.** The foundry sells provenance ("the story is the product"). The mesh ledger records who contributed what compute. The hospital model insists on de-identified archives and consent frameworks. Provenance is how each system earns trust, from buyers, patients, contributors or investors.

We call this pattern **Core, Edge, Council, Ledger (CECL)**.

## 3. A unified reference architecture

**Core.** Each participant or device holds a local store, such as SQLite with a vector column, organised as linked records: entities, events, sources and relationships. It is append-mostly and snapshotted. Rollback restores a known-good snapshot only after the current state has itself been saved, so nothing is lost silently.

**Edge.** A throttled worker indexes new material and serves peers within a strict resource budget, borrowing the 5% idle ceiling from the mobile draft. Outbound requests carry only the minimum metadata needed, never identity by default.

**Council.** A panel of role-specialised agents that must state a position, show their evidence from the Core, and record dissent. Its output is a recommendation plus a confidence range and the dissent log, never a bare verdict. A human holds the decision.

**Ledger.** An append-only record of contributions (compute, material, labour, review) and of provenance (where a casting's metal came from, which sources a recommendation cited). Whether this needs a public blockchain or a simple signed log is an open question (see section 6).

## 4. Cross-domain mappings

**Foundry × Council.** The foundry's governance has the same shape as the hospital panel. A council of agents representing participants, support workers, buyers and local council would test a proposal, such as a new furnace or a new product line, and publish the dissent alongside the decision. Participants who cannot read get the summary by voice, as the foundry's voice-first design already intends.

**Foundry × Ledger.** Each ingot or figurine carries a provenance record: collection batch, melt date, maker's mark. No personal identity is attached unless the maker chooses to sign it. The ledger makes the "ten times material value" premium checkable rather than a marketing claim.

**Companion × Mobile node.** The four-layer companion is a single-user instance of the mesh node: core, mirror, remote knowledge, bridge. Generalising it gives every phone a protected core and lets the mesh act as the "remote knowledge layer" instead of a single company's server, which reduces dependence on one provider.

**Hospital model × Mobile node.** The associative knowledge layer and the phone node's linked SQLite store are the same data model. A ward-level deployment could run entirely on local hardware inside the service, with no patient data leaving the building. That is a stronger privacy position than cloud processing, though it brings its own security obligations.

**Trading draft × Council.** The trading draft's lesson that "the risks often far outweigh the rewards" when doubling is done crudely is a general warning about recursive systems. Any agent loop that escalates commitment after a failure, whether doubling a position, retrying a clinical alert louder or re-running a failing experiment, needs a hard ceiling. The CECL Council must have bet limits in the casino sense: maximum escalation, maximum retries, and a mandatory pause for human review.

## 5. Illustrative scenarios (educational only)

*These are fictional sketches to make the architecture concrete. They describe no real person, service or outcome.*

**Scenario A, a foundry batch.** Six participants bring in a week's collection. The phone node at the workshop logs the batch weight and return-scheme receipts to the Ledger with no names. The Council (participant voice, safety, sales, finance) reviews a proposal to run a limited casting. The safety agent flags furnace ventilation as unresolved, and that dissent is recorded. The human coordinator delays the melt until ventilation is checked. The castings later sell with a provenance card showing the batch and melt date.

**Scenario B, a ward handover.** On a hypothetical inpatient unit, a nurse dictates a handover note by voice. The local Core structures it and links it to prior notes. The Council's nursing and occupational-therapy agents disagree about whether a change in sleep pattern is meaningful, and the dashboard shows the gauge as "uncertain", with the disagreement visible. The clinician decides. The system makes no diagnosis, takes no action and claims no predictive certainty. Any real version would need ethics approval, clinical governance and prospective validation before use.

**Scenario C, a mesh query.** A student's phone node lacks material on aluminium recycling chemistry. It gossips a metadata-only query, and a peer with an indexed engineering corpus answers with cited chunks. Both nodes log the exchange to the Ledger, and the student's Core keeps the answer with its provenance.

**Scenario D, an escalation ceiling.** A trading-style agent in a simulation, never with real funds, hits three consecutive losses. Instead of doubling, the CECL ceiling halts it, snapshots its state and asks for human review. The scenario exists to test the brake, not to suggest a strategy.

## 6. Open questions and failure modes

1. **Consensus is not truth.** Agents trained on similar data can agree confidently and wrongly. The Council needs genuinely diverse evidence sources and a recorded minority report, and its agreement level should never be presented as a probability of being right.
2. **Latency and performance claims.** The hospital draft's sub-16 ms deliberation and the mobile draft's resource figures are design targets. They need benchmarking on real hardware.
3. **Clinical risk.** Predicting deterioration from wearables and journaling is an active research area with mixed evidence. False positives can harm, through over-surveillance and loss of trust, and so can false negatives. Nothing in CECL should be deployed clinically without formal evaluation, consent frameworks and regulatory review.
4. **The "no skin in the game" argument cuts both ways.** A system without fatigue is also a system without accountability. Responsibility must stay with named human roles.
5. **Blockchain or signed log?** A public chain adds cost, volatility and regulatory exposure. For a pilot, a signed append-only log may be enough, and that should be tested before adding tokens.
6. **Trading strategies.** Strategies built on averaging and consolidation can suffer catastrophic loss in trending or gapping markets. No return figure should be claimed without independent, out-of-sample audit. This paper makes none.
7. **Identity minimisation versus safeguarding.** Anonymous foundry sessions protect participants but make welfare follow-up harder. That trade-off has to be designed with the participants themselves.
8. **Rollback discipline.** Systems that roll back autonomously must save the current state before restoring and must set failed runs aside rather than delete them. Otherwise "recovery" destroys evidence.

## 7. A minimal pilot path

- **Phase 0 (desk):** implement the Core schema and Ledger as SQLite plus a signed log. Simulate the Council with three agents on synthetic data only.
- **Phase 1 (foundry):** run the Council and Ledger for one real foundry workshop, covering governance and provenance only. No health data and no finance.
- **Phase 2 (mesh):** run five to ten volunteer phones sharing public corpora within the 5% idle budget. Measure battery, heat and answer quality.
- **Phase 3 (research partnership):** discuss the hospital model with a clinical research group under ethics oversight, starting with administrative burden (documentation) rather than prediction.
- **The trading draft** stays in simulation as a test bed for escalation ceilings.

## 8. Conclusion

The five drafts share one idea: keep what matters small and local, reach out only when needed, decide together with dissent on the record, and make provenance visible. Under that idea, a foundry, a phone, a ward and a companion turn out to be the same machine at different scales. The value of the CECL framing is that it makes the safety questions shared as well: escalation ceilings, rollback discipline, consensus that is not certainty, and humans who keep the decision. Those questions, not the features, are where open discussion should start.
